issue.title: A million young people not working or learning: what are they owed?
issue.question: What should the state owe a young person who is not working or learning, and what can it ask of them in return?
issue.summary: On 17 November 2026 the government published the final Milburn Young People and Work Review and its response. The review followed a rise in the number of young people not in education, employment or training to close to a million. The government says it will start locally led youth services next year, back an Opportunity and Support Guarantee, and set up a Youth Opportunities Unit reporting to the Prime Minister. It gave no new cost figures. Welfare reform steps are due in the coming weeks and a White Paper in the new year. Whether a youth allowance should be paid is a Milburn recommendation, not a decision.

news.headline: Government responds to Milburn review on young people and work, promising a new settlement for young people

poll.pollster: Ipsos (for the Department for Work and Pensions)
poll.finding: 82% agreed (49% strongly, 33% tend to) that the government should focus on supporting young people into work, education or training before it supports them through benefits. Separately, 75% said benefits should stop if a young person refuses a job because it does not interest them.

bench.title: Offer every young jobless person a real placement fast, with a fair du
bench.answer: What changes: the existing Jobs Guarantee, a fully funded six-month job, opens for under-25s after three months on Universal Credit instead of the planned 12, paid at least the legal wage. Taking a suitable offer becomes the condition of continued support, but nobody who is sick or disabled is sanctioned. Who does it: the Work and Pensions Secretary, paid for by moving money from the 2.5 billion pound Youth Guarantee and the spending on the consequences of inactivity (25 pounds for every 1 pound on opportunity), with no new tax. How we'd know: the Youth Opportunities Unit publishes quarterly, by area, how many take up offers, how many reach lasting work, and what each cost. [s1][s2]

bench.title: Give each area's youth guarantee to a local board that holds the money
bench.answer: The government would not keep this in a Prime Minister-facing Unit [s1]; it would hand the existing 2.5 billion pound Youth Guarantee [s2] to local boards, one per area, run by the council, the college and local employers. Each board would also hold the Jobs Guarantee places [s2]. The Unit would audit and publish results, not run services. How we would know: after a year, compare each area's count of young people not in education, employment or training with the national figure of close to a million [s1], and see whether the boards beat it. Citizens in the simulation backed only 6 votes for local control, so it needs proving.

bench.title: Young people steer the service and hold the purse
bench.answer: Turn the planned local youth services [s1] into cooperatives where young people using them elect most of the board. The state should fund a paid work or training place, with travel and childcare covered when needed. Councils and colleges should deliver it under that board. Employers should earn further contracts only when placements lead to lasting paid work. In return, young people able to participate should attend and follow an agreed plan, with a right to change unsuitable placements. Protect support during illness or disability. Publish costs and six-month results: who remains in paid work or learning, and whether their income covers essentials.

gate.verdict: All three answers fail or leave unclear at least one test; none passes everything. Facts check out against s1 and s2. What can't be settled by facts is how much duty, local control and cost matter against each other.

jury.question: Should a young person who is not working or learning be owed a guaranteed place first, with a duty to take it, or a local say in running the service?
options: A guaranteed place with a duty to take it up
Local boards run it with the money
Young people elect the board that runs it
None of these: pay an allowance first
jury.ruling: A guaranteed place with a duty to take it up: six of twelve simulated jurors wanted a real place waiting with a fair duty to take it, ahead of local control or an allowance.

reasons.text: Young people need a real job waiting. A duty is fair if the job is real and pays properly.
A guaranteed place with a duty. Too many sit idle and taxpayers like me pick up the bill.
Young people should steer it. Those who use a service know what's wrong with it.
They need money to live while they train. Pay an allowance first, ask later.

minister.trial: In one area, 18- to 24-year-olds on Universal Credit are offered a paid, real placement after three months, not twelve. Taking a suitable offer is the condition. Nobody sick or disabled is sanctioned. Travel and childcare are covered. Results are published every quarter.
minister.fail_number: Fewer than 4 in 10 of those offered a place are still in paid work or training six months later, against those who got no offer.
minister.statement:
A million young people. Not working, not learning. Nobody asked them what they need.
The jury picked a place with a duty. Fine. We'll start small, in one area. A real job, real pay, and a fair ask in return.
No one sick gets sanctioned. Not on my watch.
The government's own figure: 25 pounds spent on the cost of doing nothing for every 1 pound spent on a start. That is the sum that needs changing.
We publish the results every quarter. If it fails, we say so.
